MEDI2200 · Week 11 · Signalling pathways (Dr Esther Lim)

Signalling Pathways — from a molecule at the door to a changed cell

A signal is useless until something inside the cell acts on it. This guide follows one chain, reception → transduction → response, through the switches and scaffolds that control it, then through the four pathways you have to be able to draw: cAMP, PI/Ca²⁺, Ras–MAPK, PI3K–Akt, plus Wnt, which works by blocking a destruction step.

Covers all 32 slides · LO1–LO3 Figures 22 plates from the lecture Recall after every section

How to use this guide

Every subsection has a reference code like §5.3 — quote it to go deeper on exactly that piece. Each figure from your material appears as a numbered Plate with a Label Key decoding what's in it. The coloured tags carry the extras:

Reasoning
The why behind the mechanism.
Memory hook
A trick to lock it in for the exam.
Clinical / real-world
What goes wrong, and the drugs that target it.
🤔 Predict
Pause and guess before revealing — the guess is what makes it stick.
§0LO1 · What is cell signalling?

Why and how cells signal

A body of 30 trillion cells only works if they can talk to each other.

The lecture's three learning outcomes set out the guide: (1) the components and steps of signal transduction, (2) how pathways are regulated (second messengers, effectors, phosphorylation), and (3) examples of pathway types. Cells signal to communicate, to respond to intracellular changes, to respond to the extracellular environment, and to regulate cell behaviour. The cartoon in Plate 0.1 is the whole problem in one panel: two cells can't agree on a release time unless they have a way to send each other messages.

Label Key — the joke
Two cells "phoning" each other
Coordinating something like hormone release needs messages between cells, which is what cell signalling provides.
"Ten minutes?"
Timing matters. Signalling decides whether a cell responds and also when and for how long (§2).

Types of signalling — sorted by distance

The four types in Plate 0.2 differ by how far the signal travels and how it gets there:

  • Contact-dependent: needs direct contact, either through gap junctions or through a signal molecule bound to the membrane surface.
  • Autocrine/paracrine: signals travel a short distance to the target. In autocrine signalling the cell signals itself; in paracrine signalling it signals its neighbours.
  • Synaptic: neurotransmitter released across a synapse to one target cell.
  • Endocrine: hormones released into the circulation to reach distant cells.
Label Key — four routes
(A) Contact-dependent · membrane-bound signal molecule
The signal never leaves the signalling cell's surface, so only a touching neighbour is affected. This suits precise, cell-by-cell decisions in development and immunity.
(B) Paracrine · local mediator
Diffuses to nearby target cells and is quickly destroyed or taken up, so the effect stays local (e.g. inflammatory mediators).
(C) Synaptic · neuron, axon, synapse, neurotransmitter
Long-distance by wire, short-distance by chemical. This gives fast, private signalling to one target (Week 10 §2.4).
(D) Endocrine · endocrine cell, hormone, bloodstream, receptor
A broadcast to the whole body. Only cells expressing the matching receptor respond, and the response is slow but widespread.
Reasoning · broadcast vs private line

Endocrine signalling reaches every cell, so the receptor, not the route, decides who responds, and the hormone must be diluted and long-lived. Synaptic signalling uses a private line: specificity comes from the anatomy, so the transmitter can be cleared in milliseconds and the signal can be very fast. Distance, speed and specificity trade off against each other.

Components and steps

Every pathway runs the same three steps, stacked top to bottom in Plate 0.3:

  1. Reception: the signal molecule binds a receptor.
  2. Transduction: intracellular signalling proteins distribute the signal.
  3. Response: effector proteins carry out the response.
Label Key — the generic pathway
Extracellular signal molecule
The ligand: hormone, growth factor, neurotransmitter.
Receptor protein · plasma membrane of target cell
Reception. Most receptors span the membrane, so the message crosses without the ligand entering.
Intracellular signalling proteins (■ ▲ ●)
Transduction. A relay of proteins, each switching the next on.
Effector proteins
The proteins that do the work.
Metabolic enzyme → altered metabolism
E.g. glycogen breakdown.
Transcription regulatory protein → altered gene expression
A slow, lasting response.
Cytoskeletal protein → altered cell shape or movement
E.g. migration towards a chemokine.
Memory hook · "Receive, Relay, React"

Every pathway in §4–§6 maps onto the same three Rs. When drawing one in an exam, label the receptor, the relay and the effector first, then fill in the names.

R Recall — why and how
  • Contact-dependent signalling uses — gap junctions or membrane-bound signals
  • Paracrine signals travel — a short distance to nearby cells
  • Endocrine signals travel via — the circulation to distant cells
  • Synaptic signalling releases — neurotransmitter across a synapse
  • Three steps — reception, transduction, response
  • Proteins that carry out the response — effector proteins
§1LO1 · Step 1 — Reception

Reception & receptors

A cell can only hear the signals it has receptors for.

§1.1Binding a ligand

Signalling starts when a signal molecule, the ligand, binds a receptor on the target cell. Plate 1.1 shows the parts:

  • Specificity. Each receptor recognises only appropriate signals, because its binding site has a specific shape.
  • Conformational change. The receptor may change shape to bind more tightly, and that shape change is what passes the message inward.
  • Redundancy. One receptor can recognise more than one ligand if the ligands are similar.
Label Key — receptor anatomy
Ligand
The signal. It binds outside, and usually only the information crosses the membrane, not the molecule.
Ligand-binding domain
The specific pocket. Its shape decides which ligands are recognised.
Transmembrane domain
Anchors the receptor and carries the shape change across the bilayer.
Effector domain
The cytosolic part that becomes active, e.g. a kinase domain or a G-protein binding site.
Receptor–ligand complex · conformation change and downstream effects
Binding changes the receptor's shape, and the new shape is the "on" signal for the inside of the cell.
Clinical / real-world · redundancy is why drugs work

Because receptors accept similar ligands, chemists can design molecules that fit the pocket. Agonists fit and switch the receptor on (salbutamol at β₂-adrenoceptors). Antagonists fit but don't trigger the shape change, so they block the natural ligand (propranolol). The same receptor redundancy explains some side effects: a drug can bind a related receptor it was never designed for.

§1.2The main receptor classes

There are four main receptor classes, shown in Plate 1.2, and most are transmembrane proteins. Two consequences follow. A target cell can respond only to the limited set of signals it has receptors for. And the same receptor can activate several pathways to cause different effects.

Label Key — four classes, four timescales
A · Ligand-gated ion channels (e.g. cholinergic nicotinic receptors)
Effect: changes in membrane potential or ion concentration. Milliseconds, the fastest class.
B · G protein-coupled receptors (e.g. α and β adrenoceptors)
Effect: protein phosphorylation via second messengers. Seconds.
C · Enzyme-linked receptors (e.g. insulin receptors)
Effect: protein and receptor phosphorylation (R → R-PO₄). Minutes to hours when gene expression is involved.
D · Intracellular receptors (e.g. steroid receptors)
The ligand crosses the membrane itself (it is lipophilic) and binds inside. Effect: altered gene expression. Hours.
Intracellular effects
All four routes end up changing what the cell does.

The three cell-surface classes

  • Ion-channel-coupled: usually in rapid synaptic signalling.
  • G-protein-coupled: associate with a trimeric G protein.
  • Enzyme-coupled: either have enzyme activity themselves or associate with an enzyme.

Compare how each converts binding into activity in Plate 1.3.

Label Key — how each class turns on
(A) Ion-channel-coupled · signal molecule, ions, plasma membrane
Binding opens the pore, so the receptor is the effector. This makes it fast and simple.
(B) Inactive receptor / inactive G protein / inactive enzyme
Three separate proteins in the membrane.
(B) Activated receptor and G protein → activated enzyme, activated G protein
The receptor activates the G protein, which leaves to activate an enzyme. There is one extra relay step, which allows amplification (§4).
(C) Signal molecule in form of a dimer → active catalytic domain
The ligand pulls two receptors together so their built-in kinase domains activate each other (RTKs, §5).
(C) OR → activated associated enzyme
Receptors without their own catalytic domain recruit a separate enzyme (e.g. cytokine receptors with JAK kinases).
R Recall — reception
  • Receptor specificity comes from — the shape of the binding site
  • Receptor redundancy — one receptor recognises several similar ligands
  • Number of main receptor classes — four
  • Ion-channel-coupled receptors are used in — rapid synaptic signalling
  • GPCRs associate with — a trimeric G protein
  • Enzyme-coupled receptors — have enzyme activity or associate with an enzyme
  • Steroid receptors are — intracellular, act on gene expression
§2LO1 · Steps 2 & 3

Transduction & response

Relay, amplify, spread, then act fast or act slowly.

Transduction carries the signal from the receptor to the effector proteins. It uses intracellular signalling molecules, the second messengers (cAMP, Ca²⁺, IP₃, DAG). It is controlled by molecular switches that flip from inactive to active by phosphorylation or GTP binding. And it matters for amplification, regulation and divergence, the stages marked down the arrow in Plate 2.1.

Label Key — what transduction adds
Primary transduction
The receptor turns ligand binding into an intracellular change.
Relay
The message passes down a chain of proteins. Every link is a possible control point.
Modulation by other factors
Other pathways can feed in at any link and boost or damp the signal (integration).
Amplification
Each active enzyme activates many of the next, so a few ligand molecules can produce millions of product molecules.
Divergence to multiple targets
One signal fans out to several effectors at once.
Worked example · why a relay chain amplifies (illustrative numbers)

Suppose one ligand activates 1 receptor, and each enzyme step activates 10 molecules of the next (made-up, round numbers, just to show the arithmetic).

  1. Receptor → G proteins: 1 × 10 = 10 active G proteins.
  2. G proteins → adenylyl cyclase, each making ~10 cAMP: 10 × 10 = 100 cAMP.
  3. cAMP → active PKA, each phosphorylating 10 targets: 100 × 10 = 1,000 phosphorylated proteins.
  4. Each enzyme target makes 10 product molecules: 1,000 × 10 = 10,000.
  5. General form: after n steps of gain g, output = gn. Four steps of ×10 gives ×10⁴.

Answer: one ligand → ~10⁴ product molecules. Multi-step pathways buy sensitivity, which is why picomolar hormone levels can produce big effects.

Step 3 — Response

The response is the outcome of signalling, and it varies in three ways:

  • Timing and persistence: quick or slow, and of varying duration.
  • Sensitivity and range: triggered by low or high ligand concentrations, and may need a threshold.
  • Integration and coordination: may need a combination of activating and inhibiting signals.

Plate 2.2 shows where the fast/slow split comes from.

Label Key — two speeds
Extracellular signal molecule · cell-surface receptor · intracellular signalling pathway
The same front end feeds both branches.
Altered protein function — FAST (< sec to mins)
Modifies proteins that already exist (e.g. phosphorylates an enzyme), so nothing new has to be made.
Altered gene expression (DNA → RNA) — SLOW (mins to hrs)
Needs transcription, translation and often trafficking, so it is slow but lasting.
Altered cytoplasmic machinery → altered cell behaviour
Both routes end up changing what the cell does.
Reasoning · why have both speeds?

Fight-or-flight needs glucose now, so adrenaline phosphorylates existing enzymes in seconds. Adapting to a new environment (growing, differentiating) needs new proteins, which takes hours. Many signals do both: an immediate change plus a slower reprogramming that keeps it going. CREB (§4.2) and ERK (§5.3) are the "slow arms" of fast pathways.

R Recall — transduction & response
  • Four second messengers — cAMP, Ca²⁺, IP₃, DAG
  • Molecular switches activate by — phosphorylation or GTP binding
  • Transduction is important for — amplification, regulation, divergence
  • Fast response changes — protein function (seconds–minutes)
  • Slow response changes — gene expression (minutes–hours)
  • A response may require a — threshold concentration
§3LO2 · Complexity in signal regulation (I–V)

Five layers of control

Switches, place, fit, feedback, fatigue.

The lecture lists five ways a pathway is regulated: molecular switches, location, interaction specificity and affinity, feedback loops, and adaptation. Learn them as a list. Most exam questions here are "which mechanism is this?"

Memory hook · "Switch, Spot, Stick, Loop, Tire"

Switch (phosphorylation/GTP) · Spot (location/scaffolds) · Stick (affinity/docking domains) · Loop (feedback) · Tire (adaptation).

§3.1I · Molecular switches

Two switch types control whether a protein is on or off, shown side by side in Plate 3.1:

  • Phosphorylation. A protein kinase switches the protein on by phosphorylating it: it transfers a phosphate from ATP, leaving ADP. A protein phosphatase switches it off by removing the phosphate.
  • GTP binding. A GEF (guanine-nucleotide exchange factor) switches it on, because GTP is bound. A GAP (GTPase-activating protein) switches it off: GTP is hydrolysed, so GDP is bound.
Label Key — two switches, same logic
Signal in → protein kinase · ATP → ADP
Adds phosphate, so the protein is ON (P). A kinase is itself often a switch, which is how cascades form.
Protein phosphatase → Pᵢ
Removes the phosphate, so the protein is OFF. The pathway is only on while kinases outpace phosphatases.
Signal in → GTP binding (GDP out, GTP in)
Exchange, promoted by a GEF, so the protein is ON.
GTP hydrolysis → Pᵢ
The protein's own GTPase activity, sped up by a GAP, so it is OFF. The switch turns itself off.
Signal out
The ON form acts on its downstream targets.
Reasoning · why "on" must be easy to reverse

A signal is only informative if it can stop. Both switches have a built-in off route: phosphatases are always present, and GTPases hydrolyse their own GTP. So the pathway stays on only while the input keeps arriving, and the output tracks the input instead of locking on. You met the same GTPase logic in Week 10 (Sar1, ARF, Rab).

§3.2II · Location — scaffold proteins

A pathway can only switch on if all its signalling molecules are assembled in one place. Scaffold proteins have interaction domains that bind intracellular signalling proteins and hold them together. In Plate 3.2, proteins 1–2–3 sit pre-assembled on the scaffold under the receptor, so activation passes straight down the line.

Label Key — the scaffold
Inactive receptor → signal molecule → activated receptor
Ligand binding at the top.
Scaffold protein
Holds proteins 1–3 in order, close to the receptor.
Inactive → activated intracellular signalling proteins (1, 2, 3)
Each activates the next directly, with no searching through the cytosol.
Downstream signals
The output.
Reasoning · scaffolds make signals fast and private

Proteins diffusing freely would find each other slowly and could cross-activate other pathways that share components. Holding them together speeds the relay and keeps the signal in its own channel: the same kinase on two different scaffolds can serve two different pathways without crosstalk.

§3.3III · Affinity and specificity — docking domains

Intracellular signalling molecules have to interact with each other and not with other molecules. They do this through special protein domains that recognise docking sites created by phosphorylation. Phosphorylation therefore does two jobs: it switches proteins on, and it creates places for other proteins to bind. Plate 3.3 shows both kinds of docking site.

Label Key — where proteins dock
Specific phospholipid molecules (phosphoinositides) → hyperphosphorylated phosphoinositides
The activated receptor adds phosphates to membrane lipids, which then act as docking sites (the PI3K story, §5.4).
Inactive → activated intracellular signalling proteins (1, 2) → downstream signals
Proteins with lipid-binding domains (e.g. PH domains) are pulled to the membrane and activated there.
PDGF receptor · split tyrosine kinase domain
An RTK whose tail becomes phosphorylated on specific tyrosines.
P-Tyr 740 / 751 → PI 3-kinase (regulatory subunit)
Docks PI3K, which starts the survival pathway.
P-Tyr 771 → GTPase-activating protein (GAP)
Docks a Ras-GAP, which feeds back to switch Ras off.
P-Tyr 1009 / 1021 → phospholipase C-γ (PLCγ)
Docks PLC, which makes IP₃ and DAG (the same messengers as §4.3).
SH2 domains · SH3 domain
SH2 binds a phosphotyrosine plus its neighbouring residues, which gives specificity. SH3 binds proline-rich motifs and links to the next partner (Grb2 → Sos, §5.2).
Reasoning · the sequence around each tyrosine is an address

An SH2 domain doesn't recognise just "a phosphotyrosine". It reads the phosphotyrosine plus the few amino acids after it. Each tyrosine on the PDGF receptor sits in a different sequence, so each one recruits a different partner. One receptor can therefore start several pathways at once (PI3K, Ras-GAP, PLCγ), which is the "single receptor, multiple effects" point from §1.2.

§3.4IV · Positive and negative feedback

  • Positive feedback: the response promotes further signalling. It prolongs the response.
  • Negative feedback: the response inhibits further signalling. It limits the intensity of the response.

Trace the loops in Plate 3.4.

Label Key — the loops
Signal kinase (S)
The input that activates E.
Inactive E kinase ⇄ activated E kinase (P)
The output switch.
Positive feedback (red arrow back to activation)
Active E promotes its own activation, so once it passes threshold it stays on even if S fades. This is an all-or-none, memory-like response.
I (phosphatase)
The opposing enzyme that turns E off.
Negative feedback · highly active I phosphatase · DELAY
Active E switches on its own inhibitor after a delay, giving a pulse: on, then cut back. It limits intensity and can make the output oscillate.
Clinical / real-world · feedback and cancer drugs

ERK normally damps its own pathway by negative feedback (e.g. inhibiting Sos and Raf). When a tumour is treated with a BRAF or MEK inhibitor, that feedback is lost, upstream signalling surges back, and the pathway can reactivate. This is one reason targeted kinase inhibitors are often given in combination.

§3.5V · Adaptation

Prolonged exposure to a signal can reduce the response. This lets the cell stay sensitive to small changes in signal concentration on top of a high background. Plate 3.5 shows five ways to do it, from the receptor inward.

Label Key — turning the volume down
Receptor sequestration (endosome)
Receptors are endocytosed and held inside, but are recyclable, so this is quick to reverse (Week 10 §5).
Receptor down-regulation (lysosome)
Endocytosed receptors are destroyed, so the cell has fewer receptors and recovery needs new synthesis.
Receptor inactivation
The receptor stays on the surface but is blocked (e.g. phosphorylated and capped).
Inactivation of signalling protein
A downstream relay protein is switched off.
Production of inhibitory protein
The pathway induces its own brake (overlaps with negative feedback).
Clinical / real-world · tolerance and tachyphylaxis

Overusing a β₂-agonist inhaler desensitises and down-regulates β₂-adrenoceptors, so each puff works less well. Opioid tolerance arises partly the same way. This is why asthma guidelines worry about patients who rely on more and more reliever inhaler.

§3.6Putting it together — a network, not a line

A single pathway can produce several responses, but one response may need several pathways. Plate 3.6 lays out GPCR and RTK pathways side by side. Notice how they share components (PKC, Ca²⁺) and converge on the same outputs (transcription regulators, many target proteins). Sections 4 and 5 walk each column in detail.

Label Key — read each column top-down
GPCR → G protein → adenylyl cyclase → cyclic AMP → PKA
The cAMP pathway (§4.2).
GPCR → G protein → phospholipase C → IP₃ → Ca²⁺ → calmodulin → CaM-kinase
The Ca²⁺ arm of the PI pathway (§4.3).
Phospholipase C → diacylglycerol → PKC (also fed by Ca²⁺)
The DAG arm. PKC needs both DAG and Ca²⁺, a built-in AND gate.
RTK → Grb2 → Ras-GEF (Sos) → Ras → MAPKKK → MAPKK → MAP kinase
The MAPK cascade (§5.2–5.3).
RTK → PI 3-kinase → PI(3,4,5)P₃ → PDK1 → Akt kinase
The survival pathway (§5.4).
Transcription regulators / many target proteins
The two output classes (slow and fast, Plate 2.2), reached by crossing arrows from every pathway.
R Recall — regulation
  • Kinase — adds phosphate from ATP (activates)
  • Phosphatase — removes phosphate (deactivates)
  • GEF — promotes GTP binding (ON)
  • GAP — promotes GTP hydrolysis (OFF)
  • Scaffold proteins — hold signalling proteins at one location via interaction domains
  • Phosphorylated residues act as — docking sites
  • Positive feedback — prolongs the response
  • Negative feedback — limits the intensity of the response
  • Adaptation lets a cell — sense small changes despite prolonged signal
  • Five adaptation mechanisms — sequestration, down-regulation, receptor inactivation, signalling-protein inactivation, inhibitory protein
§4LO3 · G-protein-coupled receptor pathways

GPCR pathways

Seven passes, three subunits, two messengers.

Most signalling pathways are started by one of two receptor families. They share a basic plan (a receptor structure that passes the signal across the membrane, and switch-based relays), but they differ in detail:

Major types of signalling pathway
G protein-coupled receptors (GPCR)Enzyme-coupled receptors
Size of familyLargest group of cell-surface receptorsReceptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) are the most common
Typical signalsHormones and neurotransmittersGrowth factors
RegulatesSight, smell, taste, nervous systemsCell behaviour (growth, survival, differentiation)
Shared featuresSame receptor structure (7-TM); associate with a trimeric GTP-binding proteinSame receptor structure; have enzyme activity or associate with an enzyme

§4.1Activating a G protein

  1. GPCRs are 7-transmembrane receptors: the chain crosses the membrane seven times.
  2. The G protein is heterotrimeric, with α, β and γ subunits.
  3. When inactive, the G protein has GDP bound (on α).
  4. When ligand binds, the receptor acts as a GEF: Gα exchanges GDP for GTP, then dissociates from the complex. Both Gα-GTP and Gβγ go on to activate effectors.

Follow the top-to-bottom sequence in Plate 4.1.

Label Key — the G-protein cycle
GPCR · agonist · Gα (GDP), β, γ
Left inset: the 7-helix receptor with the trimer docked underneath.
Inactive GPCR · inactive G protein (α-GDP, β, γ)
The resting state, held together.
Signal molecule → activated GPCR
The receptor changes shape and pries open the α subunit.
Ras domain / AH domain of Gα → GDP released
Gα's two lobes separate and GDP escapes. This is the GEF step.
GTP binds → activated α subunit + activated βγ subunit
GTP is abundant in the cytosol, so it fills the empty site quickly. The trimer splits into two active signalling parts.
Effector activation
Gα-GTP (and Gβγ) find their targets: adenylyl cyclase (Gs) or phospholipase C (Gq).
Lipid anchors (red squiggles)
Keep α and βγ on the membrane, near their membrane-bound effectors.
Reasoning · Gα is a timer

Gα hydrolyses its own GTP within seconds and then reassociates with βγ. So the signal lasts only as long as the receptor keeps re-activating G proteins, and that only happens while ligand is bound. One active receptor can activate many G proteins in turn before the ligand leaves, which is the first amplification step.

§4.2The cAMP pathway — Gs → adenylyl cyclase → PKA → CREB

  1. Active Gα (the stimulatory Gs) binds and activates the enzyme adenylyl cyclase, which converts ATP → cyclic AMP (cAMP).
  2. cAMP (the second messenger) activates protein kinase A (PKA).
  3. Activated PKA moves into the nucleus and phosphorylates (activates) the transcription factor CREB (cAMP response element-binding protein).
  4. CREB binds the cAMP response element (CRE) to promote transcription of genes for neuropeptides, hormones and neurotrophic factors.
Label Key — cAMP to gene
Signal molecule · activated GPCR · activated α subunit of stimulatory G protein (Gs)
Reception and G-protein activation (§4.1).
Activated adenylyl cyclase · ATP → cyclic AMP
A membrane enzyme. Each active cyclase makes many cAMP molecules (amplification).
Inactive PKA → activated PKA
cAMP binds the regulatory subunits, which release the active catalytic subunits.
Cytosol · nuclear pore · nucleus
The catalytic subunits pass through nuclear pores. This is the step that turns a fast signal into a slow one (Plate 2.2).
Inactive CREB → activated, phosphorylated CREB
PKA phosphorylates CREB, which can then recruit CREB-binding protein (CBP).
Cyclic AMP response element (CRE) → activated target gene → gene transcription
The DNA sequence CREB binds, upstream of responsive genes.
Clinical / real-world · cholera toxin locks this pathway on

Cholera toxin chemically modifies Gsα so it can't hydrolyse GTP. Gs stays on, so cAMP stays high in intestinal cells. PKA keeps the CFTR Cl⁻ channel open, Cl⁻ pours into the gut, and Na⁺ and water follow: massive watery diarrhoea. The treatment is oral rehydration, which works through the Na⁺–glucose symporter you met in Week 10 (§1.3). β-blockers, by contrast, block the GPCR at the front of this pathway in the heart.

§4.3The PI (phosphatidylinositol) pathway — Gq → PLC → IP₃ + DAG

  1. The active G protein (Gq) activates membrane-bound phospholipase C (PLC).
  2. PLC cleaves the membrane lipid PIP₂ (phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate) into two messengers: IP₃ (inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate) and DAG (diacylglycerol).
  3. DAG stays in the membrane and activates protein kinase C (PKC), which phosphorylates other effector proteins.
  4. IP₃ diffuses to IP₃ receptors on the ER, which are Ca²⁺ channels. Ca²⁺ is released and controls Ca²⁺-dependent enzymes, including PKC itself.
Label Key — one lipid, two messengers
Signal molecule · activated GPCR · activated Gq protein (α-GTP, βγ)
As in Plate 4.1, but the α subunit is Gq.
Activated phospholipase C-β
The membrane enzyme Gq switches on.
PI 4,5-bisphosphate [PI(4,5)P₂]
The substrate, a phosphorylated membrane lipid.
Inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP₃)
The water-soluble head group. It diffuses through the cytosol to the ER.
Open IP₃-gated Ca²⁺-release channel · lumen of endoplasmic reticulum
An intracellular-ligand-gated channel (Week 10 Plate 2.2). Ca²⁺ stored in the ER floods out.
Diacylglycerol
The lipid tail, which stays in the membrane.
Activated protein kinase C · Ca²⁺
PKC needs DAG and Ca²⁺, so the two halves of PIP₂ are both required to activate it.
Reasoning · why split one molecule into two signals?

Cutting PIP₂ gives one water-soluble half (IP₃) that can travel to the ER and one lipid half (DAG) that stays in the membrane. One cleavage reaches two compartments at once. Because PKC needs both, it fires only when the whole pathway has run, which acts as a coincidence detector.

Clinical / real-world · Gq in smooth muscle; lithium

α₁-adrenoceptors and M₃ muscarinic receptors are Gq-coupled. IP₃-released Ca²⁺ contracts vascular and airway smooth muscle, which is why α₁-blockers lower blood pressure and M₃ antagonists (tiotropium) open the airways. Lithium blocks the enzymes that recycle inositol, damping PI signalling in overactive neurons. That is one leading explanation for its effect in bipolar disorder.

R Recall — GPCR pathways
  • GPCR structure — 7 transmembrane helices
  • G protein subunits — α, β, γ (heterotrimeric)
  • Inactive G protein has bound — GDP
  • On ligand binding, Gα — exchanges GDP for GTP and dissociates
  • Adenylyl cyclase converts — ATP to cAMP
  • cAMP activates — protein kinase A
  • PKA phosphorylates the transcription factor — CREB, which binds the CRE
  • PLC cleaves PIP₂ into — IP₃ and DAG
  • DAG activates — PKC
  • IP₃ binds receptors on the — ER, releasing Ca²⁺
§5LO3 · Enzyme-linked receptors: MAPK / PI3K

RTK pathways

Pair up, phosphorylate each other, recruit by docking, cascade.

§5.1Activating a receptor tyrosine kinase

When a ligand binds receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), four things happen in sequence (left to right in Plate 5.1):

  1. Dimerisation: a conformational change brings two receptors, and so their kinase domains, close together.
  2. The paired kinase domains activate and phosphorylate tyrosine residues on the receptor (each partner phosphorylates the other).
  3. Phosphorylation sets off a chain reaction of further phosphorylation events.
  4. The phosphorylated sites act as docking sites for adaptor proteins (§3.3).
Label Key — four frames
Inactive RTKs · tyrosine kinase domain
Separate monomers with dormant kinase domains.
Signal protein → dimer
The (often dimeric) ligand pairs the receptors.
Trans-autophosphorylation activates kinase domains
"Trans" means each receptor phosphorylates its partner, so a receptor alone can't activate itself.
Trans-autophosphorylation generates binding sites for signalling proteins
More tyrosines on the tails are phosphorylated, building the docking platform.
Activated signalling proteins (1, 2, 3) relay signal downstream
SH2-domain proteins dock and are activated (Grb2, PI3K, PLCγ).
Extracellular space / cytosol
Ligand outside, kinase activity inside.
Clinical / real-world · RTKs as cancer drivers and drug targets

Amplified HER2 (an EGF-receptor-family RTK) in ~15–20% of breast cancers means so many receptors that they dimerise without ligand. Trastuzumab (an antibody) blocks it. EGFR-mutant lung cancers respond to gefitinib/osimertinib, which block the ATP pocket of the kinase domain. Imatinib blocks the (non-receptor) tyrosine kinase BCR-ABL in CML. The insulin receptor is also an RTK; its PI3K–Akt arm (§5.4) inserts GLUT4 into muscle and fat membranes.

§5.2MAPK pathway I — Grb2 → Sos → Ras

  1. The adaptor protein Grb2 binds a receptor phosphotyrosine through its SH2 domain. Grb2 also has SH3 domains that bind Sos.
  2. Sos brings Ras into the complex. Sos is a Ras-GEF: it promotes exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras.
  3. Ras is a family of GTPases (HRAS, NRAS, KRAS). It is a molecular switch: GTP-bound = active, GDP-bound = inactive. Active Ras separates from Sos but stays attached to the plasma membrane by its lipid anchor.
Label Key — the link to Ras
Activated RTK (P)
The phosphotyrosine docking platform from Plate 5.1.
Adaptor protein (Grb2) · SH2 · SH3 SH3
A pure connector with no enzyme activity. SH2 binds the receptor, and the two SH3 domains hold Sos.
Ras-GEF (Sos)
Brought to the membrane, where Ras is. Its location is what activates it (§3.2).
Inactive Ras protein (GDP)
Anchored to the membrane by a lipid tail.
GDP out, GTP in → active Ras protein (GTP)
The GEF-driven exchange (Plate 3.1B).
Downstream signals
Active Ras turns on Raf (§5.3).
🤔 Predict · before you read on

About 1 in 4 human cancers carry a mutant Ras. Would you expect the mutation to stop Ras binding GTP, or to stop Ras hydrolysing GTP?

Stop it hydrolysing GTP. Oncogenic Ras mutations (e.g. KRAS G12) make Ras resistant to GAPs, so once it is GTP-bound it stays ON. The growth signal never switches off, and the cell keeps getting a "divide" message with no growth factor present. A Ras that couldn't bind GTP would simply be dead, not cancer-causing.

§5.3MAPK pathway II — Raf → MEK → ERK

  1. Active Ras switches on Raf (ARAF, BRAF, CRAF), which is the MAPKKK. (The slide says "phosphorylates"; mechanistically, Ras-GTP binds Raf, brings it to the membrane and activates it.)
  2. Active Raf phosphorylates MEK, the MAPKK, using ATP (→ ADP).
  3. Active MEK phosphorylates ERK, the MAPK.
  4. Active ERK phosphorylates other proteins, which either changes protein activity or starts gene transcription.
Label Key — kinase phosphorylates kinase
Active Ras protein (GTP) · plasma membrane
The membrane-bound switch at the top.
MAP kinase kinase kinase (Raf)
MAPKKK. BRAF is the commonly mutated isoform.
MAP kinase kinase (Mek) · P P
MAPKK. Needs two phosphates to be fully active.
MAP kinase (Erk) · P P
MAPK. Also dual-phosphorylated, and the final kinase.
ATP → ADP at each step
Each phosphorylation spends ATP. Three tiers give large amplification.
Protein X, protein Y → changes in protein activity
The fast arm (cytoplasmic targets).
Transcription regulatory proteins A, B → changes in gene expression
The slow arm. ERK enters the nucleus and switches on proliferation genes.
Memory hook · "Really Rapid Mitogenic Engine"

Ras → Raf → MEK → ERK. Each name loses a "kinase" as you go down: MAPKKK → MAPKK → MAPK.

Reasoning · why three kinases instead of one?

Every tier adds amplification and a control point. Because MEK and ERK each need two phosphorylations, the cascade also responds steeply: below a threshold almost nothing happens, and above it ERK switches fully on. That converts a graded growth-factor level into a clean divide/don't-divide decision (the "threshold" from §2).

Clinical / real-world · targeting the cascade

BRAF V600E is found in ~50% of melanomas and makes Raf active without Ras. Vemurafenib/dabrafenib (BRAF inhibitors) plus trametinib (a MEK inhibitor) block successive tiers. The combination delays resistance partly because of the feedback rebound described in §3.4. KRAS G12C, long thought "undruggable", now has a direct inhibitor (sotorasib).

§5.4The PI3K pathway — survival and growth

Ligand binding to an RTK also activates the PI3K pathway, which is central to cell survival and growth. It relies on phosphatidylinositols (PIs), membrane lipids that serve as second messengers or docking sites (the top half of Plate 3.3). The steps, in Plate 5.4:

  1. PI3K binds the RTK and is activated. It phosphorylates PIP₂ → PIP₃ (PI(4,5)P₂ → PI(3,4,5)P₃).
  2. PIP₃ recruits the protein kinases Akt and PDK1, which bind through their PH domains.
  3. Akt is phosphorylated by PDK1 and the mTOR complex (mTORC2).
  4. Activated Akt phosphorylates other target proteins, such as Bad.
  5. Phosphorylated Bad releases the apoptosis-inhibitory protein it was holding, which inhibits apoptosis: the cell survives.
Label Key — the survival relay
Survival signal · activated receptor tyrosine kinase
E.g. a growth factor or insulin.
Activated PI 3-kinase · PI(4,5)P₂ → PI(3,4,5)P₃
Adds a third phosphate to the inositol ring, creating the docking lipid.
PH domains · PDK1 · Akt
Pleckstrin-homology domains bind PIP₃, pulling both kinases to the same patch of membrane (location, §3.2).
Phosphorylation and activation of Akt by PDK1 and mTOR (in complex 2)
Akt needs two phosphates from two kinases, another AND gate.
Dissociation → active Akt
Leaves the membrane to find its targets.
Bad · inactive apoptosis-inhibitory protein
Unphosphorylated Bad holds the anti-apoptotic protein (e.g. Bcl-2/Bcl-xL) in an inactive complex.
Phosphorylation of Bad → inactivated Bad + 14-3-3 protein
Phospho-Bad is sequestered by 14-3-3.
Active apoptosis-inhibitory protein → inhibition of apoptosis
Freed, it blocks the cell-death machinery.
Reasoning · survival is the default only while the signal lasts

Many cells in the body need a constant survival signal; without it, unphosphorylated Bad shuts down the apoptosis inhibitor and the cell dies. That keeps cells only where they belong: a cell that drifts away from its growth-factor supply removes itself. Cancer cells often break this rule by turning the PI3K–Akt arm on permanently.

Clinical / real-world · PTEN and PI3K mutations

PTEN is the phosphatase that turns PIP₃ back into PIP₂, the "off" switch for this pathway. It is one of the most frequently lost tumour suppressors. Activating PIK3CA mutations are common in breast cancer, where the PI3Kα inhibitor alpelisib is used. mTOR inhibitors (everolimus, sirolimus) act further down this pathway as anti-cancer and immunosuppressive drugs.

Complexity in cell signalling. A cell can switch on both GPCR and RTK pathways together. They share intracellular signalling molecules and second messengers, and both control cell behaviour by changing gene transcription or protein activity. Go back to Plate 3.6 and you can now name every node.

R Recall — RTK pathways
  • First event after ligand binds an RTK — dimerisation
  • RTKs phosphorylate — tyrosine residues on the partner receptor
  • Grb2 binds phosphotyrosine via its — SH2 domain
  • Grb2 binds Sos via its — SH3 domains
  • Sos is a — Ras-GEF
  • Ras family members — HRAS, NRAS, KRAS
  • Active Ras remains bound to the — plasma membrane
  • MAPKKK, MAPKK, MAPK — Raf, MEK, ERK
  • PI3K converts — PIP₂ to PIP₃
  • Akt and PDK1 bind PIP₃ via — PH domains
  • Akt is phosphorylated by — PDK1 and mTOR complex
  • Phosphorylated Bad — releases the apoptosis-inhibitory protein → inhibits apoptosis
§6LO3 · Alternative regulation of signalling

Wnt/β-catenin — signalling by stopping destruction

The signal doesn't switch something on; it stops something being destroyed.

Wnt/β-catenin signalling controls cell fate, differentiation and proliferation. Its logic is unusual. The key effector, β-catenin, is made all the time but destroyed as fast as it is made. Wnt's job is to stop the destruction. Compare the two panels of Plate 6.1.

Label Key — off state vs on state
LRP · Frizzled (A, inactive)
The two-part Wnt receptor. Frizzled is a 7-pass receptor; LRP is a single-pass co-receptor.
Inactive Dishevelled
A cytoplasmic adaptor, idle without Wnt.
Destruction complex: axin, APC, active GSK3, active CK1
Axin and APC are scaffolds; CK1 and GSK3 are kinases. Together they phosphorylate β-catenin.
Unstable β-catenin → fragments
Phosphorylated β-catenin is ubiquitinylated and degraded by the proteasome.
LEF1/TCF · Groucho · DNA → Wnt target genes OFF
With no β-catenin, the DNA-bound TCF is held in repression by Groucho.
Wnt → activated Frizzled + activated LRP (B)
Wnt bridges the two receptors.
CK1, GSK3 → P P on LRP · Dishevelled · axin
The kinases phosphorylate LRP instead. Axin is pulled to the membrane, and the destruction complex falls apart.
Stable β-catenin → nucleus
No longer destroyed, it builds up and enters the nucleus.
β-catenin + LEF1/TCF, Groucho displaced → transcription of Wnt target genes
It converts TCF from repressor to activator.
The two states, step by step (lecture slides 30–31)
#No Wnt ligandWnt ligand present
1Frizzled and LRP receptors stay inactiveWnt binds Frizzled and LRP
2Dishevelled in the cytoplasm is inactiveFrizzled is activated and recruits and activates Dishevelled at the membrane
3Destruction complex (Axin, APC, GSK3, CK1) is activeLRP recruits and is phosphorylated by CK1 and GSK3
4β-catenin is targeted for degradation: ubiquitinylated and sent to the proteasomeAxin binds phosphorylated LRP, so the destruction complex is disrupted
5Target genes offβ-catenin is released, moves to the nucleus, and activates transcription with LEF1/TCF
Reasoning · why build a pathway on destruction?

Making β-catenin all the time and destroying it all the time looks wasteful, but it makes the pathway fast and clean. As soon as destruction stops, β-catenin builds up with no new transcription needed. As soon as Wnt goes away, the complex re-forms and β-catenin is cleared. The "brake" is the regulated part, much like the phosphatase and GAP off-routes in §3.1.

Clinical / real-world · APC and colorectal cancer

Lose APC and the destruction complex can't work. β-catenin accumulates with no Wnt present, and TCF target genes (proliferation genes such as MYC) stay on. Inherited APC mutation causes familial adenomatous polyposis (hundreds of colon polyps and near-certain cancer without colectomy), and APC loss is an early step in most sporadic colorectal cancers. Lithium inhibits GSK3, so it partly mimics a Wnt signal, which is another of its many effects.

Memory hook · "No Wnt, no β-catenin"

Without Wnt the complex (Axin, APC, GSK3, CK1, "Two As, G and C") is on and β-catenin is destroyed. With Wnt the complex is pulled apart at LRP and β-catenin survives to switch on genes.

R Recall — Wnt and the big picture
  • Wnt receptors — Frizzled and LRP
  • Destruction complex — Axin, APC, GSK3, CK1
  • Without Wnt, β-catenin is — ubiquitinylated and degraded by the proteasome
  • With Wnt, LRP is phosphorylated by — CK1 and GSK3
  • Axin binds phospho-LRP, so the destruction complex is — disrupted
  • β-catenin activates transcription with — LEF1/TCF
  • Wnt signalling regulates — cell fate, differentiation, proliferation
  • Phosphorylation creates — docking sites that help proteins assemble
  • Most pathways start at — GPCRs or enzyme-linked receptors
